common_name: Swans in Flight Siberian Iris (Morgan-Wood and Historic 2016 Dykes Medal White Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Swans in Flight is a large-flowered white Siberian iris with yellow markings.

directions: Plant divisions in spring or shortly after bloom in consistently moist, humus-rich soil, setting crowns no deeper than they grew previously. Swans in Flight was hybridized by Robert Hollingworth and registered in 2006, producing large, rounded white flowers accented with yellow signal markings on sturdy 30-to-36-inch stems. It won the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal in 2013, the top honor for Siberian irises, and then went on to win the overall American Dykes Medal in 2016, becoming the first beardless iris in the award's history to win the Society's highest honor. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or late summer to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Perry Dyer Arilbred Iris (2024 Dykes Medal Palest Lavender and Cream Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in sharply drained soil; Perry Dyer is an oncobred (OGB-) arilbred iris with palest lavender standards and cream-lavender falls marked by a dark plum-wine spot.

directions: Set rhizomes shallowly with the top surface exposed in gritty, sharply drained soil, since arilbred irises are especially prone to rot in heavy or wet ground. Perry Dyer was hybridized by Paul Black, registered in 2017 as seedling T132F, a sibling of 'Galaxina', with palest lavender standards and cream-lavender falls fading to near white around a dark plum-wine spot and a grey-based, brown-tipped beard. After earning the Franklin Cook Cup and the William Mohr Medal, it won the American Dykes Medal in 2024. Divide congested clumps every two to three years after bloom and allow the exposed rhizome tops to bake in full sun.

common_name: Alabama Blue Fin Pseudata Iris (2026 Dykes Medal Blue Species-Cross Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Alabama Blue Fin is a pseudata (Iris ensata x Iris pseudacorus lineage) iris that tolerates boggy soil or shallow standing water.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in rich, organic soil kept consistently moist to wet, since pseudata irises descend from both the bog-loving Iris ensata and the wetland Iris pseudacorus. Alabama Blue Fin was bred by Jill Copeland from a cross of seedling GXS-2 ('Gubijin' x 'Sushi') with 'Christina's Sister' and registered in 2016, producing blue-toned flowers on stems reaching about 38 inches. After collecting an Award of Merit, the Fred and Barbara Walther Cup, and the Randolph Perry Medal, it became hybridizer Jill Copeland's first American Dykes Medal winner in 2026. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring, keeping the planting site reliably damp through the growing season.

common_name: So Van Gogh Siberian Iris (Morgan-Wood Medal Bicolor Blue-Violet and Yellow Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; So Van Gogh was promoted by its breeders as the first distinctly bicolor Siberian iris.

directions: Plant divisions in spring or right after bloom in humus-rich soil that holds moisture without becoming waterlogged. So Van Gogh was hybridized by Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks and registered in 2005, with medium blue-violet standards and style arms over yellow falls that lighten at the edges and darken near the signal, a striking two-tone pattern its breeders called the first truly bicolor Siberian iris. It won the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal in 2012. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or late summer to keep the rhizomes vigorous.

common_name: Ships Are Sailing Siberian Iris (Morgan-Wood Medal Bluebird-Blue Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Ships Are Sailing bears lightly ruffled bluebird-blue flowers with a small gold signal.

directions: Plant divisions in spring or shortly after flowering in fertile soil that stays evenly moist through the growing season. Ships Are Sailing was hybridized by Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks and registered in 1998, bearing light blue standards shaded and veined deeper bluebird blue and darker bluebird-blue falls edged in light blue around a small gold signal heavily veined in blue-violet, carried on vigorous, floriferous 35-inch stems. It earned an Award of Merit before winning the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal in 2007. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring or late summer to sustain strong bloom.

common_name: Strawberry Fair Siberian Iris (Ruffled Crushed-Strawberry Pink Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Strawberry Fair bears crushed-strawberry pink, heavily ruffled falls with a small white signal.

directions: Plant divisions in spring or right after bloom in humus-rich soil kept consistently moist. Strawberry Fair was hybridized by Robert Hollingworth and registered in 1992, carrying short lavender-pink standards over heavily ruffled, crushed-strawberry pink falls set off by a small white signal, blooming late in the Siberian iris season. It went on to win the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal in 2001. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or late summer to keep plants blooming vigorously.

common_name: Ruffles and Flourishes Siberian Iris (Morgan-Wood Medal Red-Violet Tetraploid Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Ruffles and Flourishes is a tetraploid Siberian iris with ruffled red-violet flowers edged in white.

directions: Plant divisions in spring or shortly after bloom in fertile, evenly moist soil. Ruffles and Flourishes was hybridized by Robert Hollingworth and registered in 2002, a tetraploid cultivar with ruffled red-violet falls rimmed in a thin white wire edge around a gold signal haloed in blue, blooming mid-to-late season on 33-inch stems. After an Award of Merit in 2007, it won the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal in 2009. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring or late summer to maintain vigor.

common_name: Garnet Slippers Intermediate Bearded Iris (Sass Medal Burgundy and Red-Black Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Garnet Slippers is an intermediate bearded iris with burgundy standards over red-black falls and mandarin-red beards.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil. Garnet Slippers was hybridized by Keith Keppel from seedling 97-47C and registered in 2004, producing burgundy standards and greyed-burgundy style arms blended with golden tan, over red-black falls and mandarin-red beards on compact 20-inch stems. After an Honorable Mention and an Award of Merit, it won the American Iris Society's Hans and Jacob Sass Medal in 2011. Divide congested clumps every two to three years after bloom to keep the smaller median rhizomes from overcrowding.

common_name: Rimaround Intermediate Bearded Iris (Sass Medal White Plicata Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Rimaround is an intermediate bearded iris with white plicata falls stitched in purple.

directions: Set rhizomes shallowly with the top surface exposed to the sun in loose, well-drained soil. Rimaround was hybridized by J. Terry Aitken from a cross of 'Art Deco' and 'Fairy Ring' and registered in 2007, bearing white standards and falls heavily stitched in purple plicata patterning with a round purple band near the edge of the falls and beards tipped purple, on 22-inch stems blooming mid-to-late season. After an Honorable Mention and an Award of Merit, it won the American Iris Society's Hans and Jacob Sass Medal in 2013. Divide congested clumps every two to three years after bloom.

common_name: Cat In The Hat Intermediate Bearded Iris (Sass Medal Raspberry-Rose Plicata Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Cat In The Hat is an intermediate bearded iris with raspberry-rose plicata bands over a cream ground.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil. Cat In The Hat was hybridized by Paul Black and registered in 2009, with mid-raspberry-rose standards finely veined in dark violet-blue over cream falls banded in wide raspberry-rose plicata markings with darker hafts and orange beards tipped white, blooming late midseason to very late on 27-inch stems. After an Honorable Mention and an Award of Merit, it won the American Iris Society's Hans and Jacob Sass Medal in 2018. Divide congested clumps every two to three years after bloom to keep median rhizomes from crowding.
